paragraphs: Stochastic optimization methods make updates using randomness, so understanding their long-run behavior requires more than analyzing a single deterministic sequence. This paper develops a shared convergence theorem that can support several algorithms. Instead of building a separate argument for each method, researchers can check a collection of representative conditions.

The theorem covers convergence in expectation and almost sure convergence. These describe behavior averaged over randomness and behavior holding with probability one, respectively. As applications, the authors recover results for stochastic gradient descent and random reshuffling in more general settings, showing that the framework can consolidate and extend existing analyses.

The paper also establishes new results for stochastic proximal gradient and stochastic model-based methods on nonsmooth, nonconvex problems. These are settings where the objective need not be smoothly differentiable or have a simple global shape. The contribution is a reusable route to convergence guarantees: its reach depends on verifying the theorem's conditions for the method under consideration.
neurips-2022-a-unified-convergence-theor.tldr: A shared theorem yields expected and almost sure convergence guarantees for several stochastic optimization methods when its conditions hold.

paragraphs: Active learning aims to learn efficiently by choosing which observations to collect. In an interactive setting, however, the most informative decision may not satisfy the relevant safety requirements. This paper studies the difficulty of identifying the best safe decision when the safety constraints themselves are initially unknown.

The authors express the task as a safe linear bandit problem, where candidate decisions are called arms. Their algorithm uses adaptive experimental design to decide what evidence to gather. A central idea is to balance two reasons for rejecting an arm: it may violate safety constraints, or it may simply be worse than another acceptable choice.

The analysis shows that the algorithm efficiently trades off the difficulty of establishing these two conclusions. This matters because spending effort proving an arm inferior may be unnecessary if it can instead be ruled out as unsafe. The authors also report good performance on synthetic and real-world datasets, supporting the practical relevance of their approach to identifying a best arm under safety constraints.
neurips-2022-active-learning-with-safety.tldr: An adaptive learning algorithm identifies the best safe decision by balancing evidence that alternatives are unsafe or suboptimal.

paragraphs: A model-based reinforcement learning agent needs an environment model that supports useful planning. Value equivalence formalizes this by requiring the model to reproduce particular value updates for chosen functions and policies. Its exact equalities are restrictive, especially when the functions involved can only be approximated during learning.

This paper introduces approximate value equivalence, replacing exact agreement with permitted error. With a sufficiently large tolerance, approximate equivalence relative to one function set extends to another. This connection lets the authors derive planning-performance bounds for value-equivalent models defined using arbitrary function sets, broadening the situations that the theory can address.

The relaxed framework also exposes a practical tradeoff involving model capacity. Learning to match more functions can demand more than a limited model can represent accurately. The authors empirically identify situations where concentrating on a smaller function set produces a better choice than fitting a larger set less accurately. This is a conditional finding about limited-capacity agents, rather than a rule that smaller sets always improve planning.
neurips-2022-approximate-value-equivalen.tldr: Approximate value equivalence allows modeling error and reveals when limited-capacity agents benefit from accurately matching fewer value functions.

paragraphs: Processing very long sequences requires a way to carry information forward without making computation grow too quickly. The Block-Recurrent Transformer applies a transformer layer repeatedly along a sequence while maintaining recurrent state. Its complexity grows linearly with sequence length, and its training unit is a block of tokens.

Working on blocks allows parallel computation within each block, making the design suitable for accelerator hardware. The recurrent cell uses self-attention and cross-attention to update tokens and a large collection of state vectors. It also incorporates gates inspired by LSTMs, extending that recurrent design to a substantially larger state representation.

The authors report that their implementation of recurrence matches a conventional transformer layer in computation time and parameter count while substantially improving perplexity on very long language-modeling sequences. Against a long-range Transformer XL baseline, their model performs better and runs twice as fast. Evaluations cover books, scientific papers, and source code, supporting the usefulness of combining blockwise attention with persistent state across different kinds of long text.
neurips-2022-block-recurrent-transformer.tldr: A transformer that recurrently processes token blocks improves long-sequence language modeling while keeping complexity linear in sequence length.

paragraphs: Matching facial features across species is difficult because animal data are relatively scarce, correspondences are ambiguous, and face shapes and appearances vary widely. Dense Interspecies Face Embedding seeks shared facial features across animals, including humans. The goal is to establish meaningful associations despite these large differences in visual form.

The method addresses the obstacles with three components. It distills knowledge from CSE and StyleGAN2 without requiring additional data or labels. It then explores StyleGAN2's latent space to synthesize image pairs that provide possible cross-species associations. A semantic matching loss helps the model handle substantial differences in facial shape.

The authors quantitatively evaluate facial keypoint transfer between species on MAFL and AP-10K, using approaches such as unsupervised keypoint detection for comparison. They also present applications to interspecies face manipulation and dense keypoint transfer. Together, these applications show how a common facial representation can support both locating corresponding features and manipulating images, with knowledge transfer and generated pairs supplying the learning signals.
neurips-2022-dense-interspecies-face-emb.tldr: DIFE combines knowledge distillation, generated image pairs, and semantic matching to learn facial correspondences across species.

paragraphs: Many datasets describe relationships between two kinds of entities, such as documents and terms or genes and disorders. A bipartite graph represents these two sides and the connections between them. Biclustering seeks groups across both sides, allowing the structure of their relationships to guide how the data are organized.

This paper proposes a scalable biclustering model built on optimal transport. The model generalizes several classical biclustering approaches, placing them within a broader formulation. That connection matters because the contribution is both a new approach to grouping paired data and a framework that encompasses established ways of expressing the problem.

The authors evaluate the method extensively against other optimal-transport biclustering algorithms, examining results along both dimensions of the datasets. Their experiments support the validity of the approach for the paired-data setting. Assessing both sides is central to the task: a useful biclustering method must account for the organization of each entity type as well as the relationships linking the two.
neurips-2022-efficient-and-effective-opt.tldr: A scalable optimal-transport model generalizes classical biclustering approaches and is evaluated on both sides of paired datasets.

paragraphs: Data augmentation encourages a reinforcement learning agent to treat certain transformed observations consistently. That can support generalization, but the paper observes that teaching this consistency during reinforcement learning can interfere with training and reduce sample efficiency. Because learning conditions change over time, an agent can also forget an earlier consistency prior.

The authors develop a separate network-distillation method that can inject the prior at different times, including after reinforcement learning finishes. Their scheduling framework first emphasizes success in the training environments. It adaptively chooses which augmentation to use, with the option to use none, rather than requiring a fixed augmentation throughout training.

Afterward, distillation draws remaining generalization benefits from all the augmentations without collecting additional samples. Experiments demonstrate the utility of this framework, particularly its ability to postpone augmentation until the end of reinforcement learning. The central implication is that when an agent learns an augmentation-induced prior matters alongside which augmentation is chosen: useful consistency information can still disrupt learning if introduced at an unsuitable time.
neurips-2022-efficient-scheduling-of-dat.tldr: Adaptive augmentation scheduling and later distillation help separate reinforcement learning progress from learning consistency priors for generalization.

paragraphs: A symmetric function on a set produces the same result regardless of the order in which the elements are presented. Neural architectures can build this symmetry into their design, but sharing that property does not mean they represent functions equally efficiently. This paper compares the expressive efficiency of Relational Networks and DeepSets.

The authors treat the Relational Network architecture as a natural generalization of DeepSets and construct a function that separates their capabilities. The function acts on sets containing N elements, each with D dimensions. Under a restriction to analytic activation functions, a Relational Network can approximate it efficiently.

For DeepSets, approximating the constructed function provably requires width exponential in N and D. This establishes a potentially enormous representation-cost difference between the architectures even though both handle symmetric functions. The result is an existence statement with a stated activation restriction: it identifies a function exposing a strong architectural gap, rather than claiming that every set-processing task needs exponentially larger DeepSets models.
neurips-2022-exponential-separations-in-.tldr: With analytic activations, a constructed symmetric function is efficiently approximated by Relational Networks but requires exponentially wide DeepSets.

paragraphs: Estimating what would happen after an intervention is a central problem in causal inference. Pearl's front-door criterion offers one strategy for identifying such effects from data. Its definition tells researchers whether a proposed set of variables qualifies, but that leaves a practical search problem: which sets should they consider?

This paper provides algorithms that find and enumerate sets satisfying the front-door criterion in a supplied causal diagram. Finding a valid set makes the criterion actionable when researchers have not already selected one. Enumerating the alternatives goes further by exposing multiple possible ways to formulate an identifiable causal-effect estimation task.

Those alternatives matter because mathematically valid choices can differ in practical desirability. The authors highlight measurement cost, feasibility, and statistical power as considerations that can guide selection. The contribution therefore connects a graphical criterion to the decisions involved in applying it: researchers can search for qualifying sets and compare available options using properties relevant to their study, within the given causal diagram.
neurips-2022-finding-and-listing-front-d.tldr: New algorithms find and enumerate front-door adjustment sets, helping researchers choose practical options for causal-effect estimation.

paragraphs: In structured multi-label prediction, labels can have logical relationships: one may imply another, while two others may exclude each other. Predicting labels separately can conflict with those relationships. This paper incorporates the constraints into a geometric representation of labels so that logical structure directly shapes the prediction problem.

The method uses the hyperbolic Poincaré ball and represents labels with hyperplanes that serve as decision boundaries. Interpreting them through convex regions makes the logic geometric. A region contained inside another expresses implication, while disjoint regions express mutual exclusion. The authors provide theoretical grounding for preserving these relationships in the embedding space.

Across 12 datasets, the experiments report significant improvements in mean average precision, fewer constraint violations, and an order of magnitude fewer dimensions than the baselines. These findings connect predictive performance, logical consistency, and representation size. The reported reduction in violations is an empirical improvement, while the geometric construction supplies the structural mechanism intended to keep related label decisions consistent.
neurips-2022-hyperbolic-embedding-infere.tldr: Hyperbolic label regions encode implication and exclusion, improving prediction quality and reducing logical violations in experiments.

paragraphs: Human image labels can contain mistakes or reflect genuine ambiguity. Combining annotations into a single label can discard that information and lower data quality. This paper introduces a benchmark with nine real-world datasets and multiple annotations per image to study how labeling effort affects the data used to train classifiers.

The benchmark separates evaluation into two phases. First, a method improves the labels; second, a fixed model evaluates the resulting data. This arrangement lets researchers compare labeling and learning approaches through a shared evaluation procedure. It also supports studying how annotation costs relate to the performance of supervised and semi-supervised methods.

Across thousands of experiments, the authors find that multiple annotations better approximate the underlying class distribution than a single annotation. They also identify a problem with hard labels: assigning one definitive class cannot capture ambiguity in the data. This may contribute to overconfident models. The results motivate treating label creation as a substantive learning problem, with attention to uncertainty and annotation effort.
neurips-2022-is-one-annotation-enough-a-.tldr: A nine-dataset benchmark shows how multiple annotations better represent image-label ambiguity and support studying labeling effort versus model performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning Nash equilibria in two-player, zero-sum Markov games, where decisions influence an evolving state. It represents action values using a function from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The main challenge is exploration: the learner must gather useful information in a high-dimensional space of possible value functions.

The proposed online algorithm seeks an equilibrium by minimizing the duality gap, a measure of the remaining gap between the players' opposing optimization objectives. Upper and lower confidence bounds guide exploration using optimism under uncertainty. Under assumptions on rewards and game dynamics described as mild, the authors prove regret of order square root of T and polynomial computational complexity.

The paper also develops extensions with different strengths. One uses a Bernstein-type bonus to obtain a tighter regret bound. Another addresses model misspecification and can be applied to neural-network function approximation. Together, these results connect uncertainty-guided exploration with computational and learning guarantees, while extending the approach toward situations where the chosen function model does not exactly match the game.
neurips-2022-learning-two-player-markov-.tldr: An uncertainty-guided algorithm learns equilibria in zero-sum Markov games with nonlinear value approximation and provable regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Domain generalization aims to transfer learning from several observed domains to an unseen one. Separating shared meaning from domain-specific variation is difficult because these factors can be intertwined. Mix and Reason approaches the problem by encouraging stable relationships among semantic features, described as the structural invariance of semantic topology.

Its first component, Category-aware Data Mixing, combines images from different domains using activation maps generated by two complementary classification losses. This encourages attention to semantic objects. Its second component, Adaptive Semantic Topology Refinement, represents semantic relationships with graphs and progressively refines them through local feature aggregation and global reasoning across domains.

The two components address related aspects of generalization: the image mixing directs learning toward meaningful content, while graph-based reasoning refines how that content is related across domains. Experiments on multiple domain-generalization benchmarks support the framework's effectiveness and robustness. The approach offers a way to pursue shared semantic structure without relying on a clean division of representations into two disjoint parts, an assumption the authors identify as restrictive.
neurips-2022-mix-and-reason-reasoning-ov.tldr: Mix and Reason combines category-aware image mixing with graph-based semantic refinement to improve generalization to unseen domains.

paragraphs: Word embeddings can require substantial storage, creating a deployment obstacle on devices with limited resources. MorphTE compresses these representations using word morphology. Its building blocks are morphemes, the smallest word units that carry meaning or grammatical function, so the compressed representation incorporates linguistic structure into how embeddings are constructed.

The method combines morpheme vectors through tensor products to represent a word embedding. This introduces prior semantic and grammatical knowledge while using smaller vectors and a smaller inventory of units than full-word representations require. The same construction therefore serves two purposes: reducing the embedding parameter count and connecting words to their meaningful components.

The authors conduct experiments on tasks including machine translation and question answering. On four translation datasets spanning different languages, they report roughly twentyfold compression of word-embedding parameters without performance loss and significant improvements over related compression methods. The stated result concerns the embedding parameters, and it supports the possibility of retaining translation performance while making that part of the model substantially smaller.
neurips-2022-morphte-injecting-morpholog.tldr: MorphTE builds word embeddings from tensor-combined morpheme vectors, achieving about twentyfold embedding compression without performance loss on four translation datasets.

paragraphs: Saliency maps highlight input regions presented as important to a network's prediction. A common evaluation keeps the highest-ranked pixels, replaces the others, and checks whether the prediction remains similar. This paper argues that treating success on that test as a causal explanation can be questionable because the evaluation captures only part of what an explanation should establish.

Drawing on completeness and soundness from logic, the authors distinguish two requirements and introduce metrics addressing both. Existing masking-based evaluations emphasize completeness while overlooking soundness. The new framework remains intrinsic: it uses the dataset and the network itself, without requiring separate trained models or human judgments to evaluate the explanations.

The authors also describe a simple saliency method that matches or outperforms previous methods under their evaluations. Their experiments suggest soundness-based explanations for why common practices such as total-variation regularization and upsampling can help. The contribution thus links improved evaluation criteria with practical method design, while questioning whether preserving a prediction alone adequately validates a saliency map.
neurips-2022-new-definitions-and-evaluat.tldr: New intrinsic saliency evaluations assess both completeness and soundness, exposing weaknesses in prediction-preserving masking tests.

paragraphs: Combinatorial black-box optimization searches among discrete possibilities using evaluations of an unknown objective. The search space can grow explosively, and its candidates need not have a useful natural ordering. This paper adapts tree-search and partitioning techniques to organize that space and develop solvers with theoretical performance guarantees.

The first algorithm, Optimistic Lipschitz Tree Search, assumes the objective's Lipschitz constant is known. This constant constrains how sharply function values can vary. Under specific conditions, the authors establish linear convergence rates, improving on the logarithmic rates of the baselines considered. The stronger rate therefore comes with explicit conditions and an information requirement.

The second algorithm, Optimistic Combinatorial Tree Search, adapts to the more realistic situation where the Lipschitz constant is unknown. The authors prove similar theoretical guarantees and provide numerical comparisons with state-of-the-art methods on typical benchmarks. The combined contribution is a route from a solver using known regularity information to an adaptive version, with experiments illustrating the potential of tree-based search for discrete black-box problems.
neurips-2022-optimistic-tree-searches-fo.tldr: Two optimistic tree-search algorithms offer conditional convergence guarantees for combinatorial black-box optimization, with and without a known Lipschitz constant.

paragraphs: As a rodent moves through a place cell's field, the cell can fire progressively earlier within successive theta cycles, a pattern called phase precession. Some cells also show phase procession, a shift in the opposite direction. This paper proposes a neural circuit mechanism that accounts for both patterns within one model.

The model is a continuous attractor neural network with feedback inhibition, inspired by interactions between the hippocampus and medial septum. Feedback creates an internal tendency for the network's activity bump to move. This competes with movement driven by external input, producing an oscillatory tracking state in which the represented position sweeps around the animal's physical position.

In the model, forward and backward sweeps explain precession and procession at the level of individual neurons. Adjusting feedback-inhibition strength also accounts for cells showing both patterns and cells showing mainly precession. The contribution is a proposed circuit-level explanation connecting moving population activity to firing timing, offering a mechanism for interpreting hippocampal temporal coding.
neurips-2022-oscillatory-tracking-of-con.tldr: A continuous attractor model with feedback inhibition explains both directions of place-cell theta phase shifts through oscillatory position tracking.

paragraphs: Robustness certificates establish conditions under which adversarial changes cannot alter a model's prediction. Existing randomized-smoothing certificates for graph neural networks can be overly pessimistic because they ignore how these networks operate. This paper uses the message-passing architecture to derive certificates that account for how adversarial influence travels through a graph.

The method randomly intercepts messages and analyzes the probability that information from adversarially controlled nodes reaches a target node. This supports guarantees against attackers controlling entire nodes and arbitrarily changing their features. The analysis uses architectural knowledge, making it a gray-box approach rather than treating the prediction system as an opaque function.

The certificates become stronger for attacks originating farther away, because messages traveling from more distant nodes are more likely to be intercepted. Experiments across models and datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The authors also show that graph sparsification can significantly improve certifiable robustness. This connects the guarantee to graph structure: changing the available communication pathways can strengthen the protection that the analysis can establish.
neurips-2022-randomized-message-intercep.tldr: Randomly intercepting graph messages enables stronger architecture-aware robustness certificates against nodes with arbitrarily manipulated features.

paragraphs: Network rank describes information flowing through a neural network, and low-rank representations have motivated many architectural ideas. This paper investigates why rank deficiency arises within deep networks. Its focus is the mechanism behind reduced representational independence as functions and network blocks are composed across layers.

Using rules of differential and algebraic composition, the authors establish a universal monotone nonincreasing property of network ranks. They also identify rank deficiency associated with network blocks and deep function coupling. Numerical tools allow them to examine layer-by-layer rank behavior in ResNets, deep multilayer perceptrons, and Transformers on ImageNet, with findings consistent with the theory.

The paper further identifies an independence deficit in classification outputs. Because of rank deficiency, the confidence assigned to a category can be determined linearly from the confidences of a small number of other categories. This ties an internal structural property to relationships among predictions. Together, the theoretical and empirical results offer an explanation of how deep composition can restrict independent information within a network.
neurips-2022-rank-diminishing-in-deep-ne.tldr: Theory and layerwise measurements connect diminishing network rank with reduced independence among deep-network classification confidences.

paragraphs: Adversarial image changes are often defined at the pixel level, where their meaning can be difficult to interpret. This paper studies attacks created by manipulating an image generator's latent representations. Such feature-level changes can be perceptible and interpretable, making the resulting images useful for investigating what a classifier has learned.

The authors demonstrate a wide range of attacks at ImageNet scale, including targeted, universal, disguised, physically realizable, and black-box attacks. These results establish the versatility and robustness of feature-level adversaries in the settings studied. Their interpretability also gives the attacks a diagnostic role beyond merely producing incorrect classifications.

The authors use adversarial images to predict spurious associations between visual features and classes. They then test those predictions with copy-and-paste attacks, inserting one natural image into another to induce a targeted misclassification. This connects an observed failure to a testable hypothesis about the network's representations. The results suggest that feature-level attacks can support rigorous interpretability work and help diagnose brittle feature associations.
neurips-2022-robust-feature-level-advers.tldr: Interpretable feature-level attacks reveal spurious feature–class associations that can be tested through targeted copy-and-paste image attacks.

paragraphs: In streaming best-arm identification, options arrive one at a time, rewards are unknown, and only a limited number of options can be retained. The learner seeks the highest-reward arm while minimizing memory and sampling. This paper asks whether sampling can adapt to each instance's individual reward gaps while memory remains small.

The authors prove a strong single-pass tradeoff: achieving the stated instance-sensitive sampling bound requires memory linear in the number of arms; otherwise sampling must be asymptotically higher. Lower bounds persist under stronger assumptions, including random arrival order or knowledge of all reward gaps. However, when all the strong assumptions hold together, a proposed algorithm achieves instance-optimal sampling while storing one arm.

The proofs introduce an arm-trapping lemma concerning the easier-looking task of retaining the best arm's index among a sublinear number of candidates. It establishes a sampling requirement scaling with the number of arms divided by the squared best-versus-second-best gap. Because this result also applies outside streaming, it provides a broader tool for studying sampling and memory tradeoffs.
neurips-2022-single-pass-streaming-lower.tldr: Single-pass bandit exploration faces strong memory–sampling tradeoffs for instance-sensitive guarantees, with a one-arm-memory exception under combined strong assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately gradient descent can solve inverse problems from randomly sampled, noisy observations. It measures error using Sobolev norms and considers a broad family of training objectives. That family includes Sobolev training for kernel regression, Deep Ritz Methods, and physics-informed neural networks for elliptic partial differential equations.

The analysis uses a suitable reproducing kernel Hilbert space, allowing a potentially infinite-dimensional model. Kernel integral operators describe varying levels of problem difficulty. Within this framework, the authors prove that gradient descent can attain statistical optimality and that the optimal number of passes through the data increases with sample size.

The theory also explains an implicit acceleration associated with training using a Sobolev norm. As both dataset size and task difficulty increase, it implies that Deep Ritz Methods need more epochs at their optimal stopping point than physics-informed neural networks, although both can be statistically optimal. This distinguishes the accuracy attainable from the data from the training effort needed to reach it under the analyzed objectives.
neurips-2022-sobolev-acceleration-and-st.tldr: A unified analysis links statistically optimal gradient-descent solutions of elliptic inverse problems to objective-dependent training duration and Sobolev acceleration.

paragraphs: Under covariate shift, source and target domains have different input distributions while their output distributions conditional on the input remain similar. This paper studies transfer learning for linear regression in that setting. It analyzes pretraining on source examples followed by finetuning on target examples, with online stochastic gradient descent used for both stages.

The authors derive sharp upper and lower bounds on excess prediction risk that depend on the particular problem instance. For a large class of instances, the bounds suggest that source data scaling as O(N²), with little or no target data, can match supervised learning using N target examples. This quantifies how source data can substitute for target observations.

The theory also shows that even a small target dataset for finetuning could drastically reduce the source-data requirement. Thus, target examples can matter both as direct training information and as a way to make pretraining more effective. These conclusions concern the analyzed linear-regression instances under covariate shift, where distribution differences determine the benefits and limits of transfer.
neurips-2022-the-power-and-limitation-of.tldr: Instance-dependent bounds explain when source pretraining can replace target data and how limited finetuning can sharply reduce source-data needs.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search automates network design, but evaluating candidate architectures through training can be expensive. Training-free metrics aim to make search more scalable. This paper addresses a theoretical gap around gradient-based versions of these metrics: how they relate, why they work empirically, and how their strengths might be combined more effectively.

The authors present a unified theoretical analysis that studies relationships among the metrics and provides guarantees concerning their generalization performance. Bringing the measures into one framework makes their behavior more interpretable and supplies a basis for improving search. The analysis is then used to develop hybrid neural architecture search, called HNAS.

HNAS aims to combine the search efficiency associated with training-free methods and the search effectiveness associated with training-based methods. Extensive experiments demonstrate these advantages and show consistent improvements to training-free search in the evaluated settings. The contribution connects theory to algorithm design: the framework uses the shared analysis to guide a hybrid approach, rather than treating existing metrics as unrelated empirical scoring rules.
neurips-2022-unifying-and-boosting-gradi.tldr: A unified theory of gradient-based training-free architecture metrics motivates HNAS, a hybrid search framework combining efficiency with effective architecture selection.

paragraphs: VRL3 organizes visual reinforcement learning into three stages that draw on different kinds of data. First, ordinary image datasets teach a visual representation without tying it to a particular control task. Second, offline reinforcement learning data, such as a limited set of expert demonstrations, adapt that representation to the task.

The third stage finetunes the agent through online reinforcement learning. This sequence gives general visual learning, task-specific adaptation, and direct interaction distinct roles. Alongside the framework, the authors analyze obstacles to data-driven visual reinforcement learning and present design principles and findings intended to explain how these data sources can work together.

On challenging hand-manipulation tasks with sparse rewards and realistic visual inputs, the authors report an average 780% improvement in sample efficiency over the previous state of the art. On the hardest task, the reported gain is 1220%, rising to 2440% with a wider encoder, while solving the task uses 10% of the computation. These results demonstrate substantial gains for the evaluated tasks and support further use of staged, data-driven learning.
neurips-2022-vrl3-a-data-driven-framewor.tldr: VRL3 combines image pretraining, offline reinforcement learning, and online finetuning to substantially improve sample efficiency on challenging visual manipulation tasks.
